title: The Ten Commandments
summary: God speaks the Ten Commandments to all Israel, beginning with who he is and what he has done: the LORD who brought them out of the house of slavery. The commands forbid other gods, idols, and the misuse of his name, set apart the Sabbath, and protect parents, life, marriage, property, truth, and the neighbor from our desires. Terrified by the thunder and smoke, the people ask Moses to speak to them instead, and God gives the first laws of worship: no gods of silver or gold, and a plain altar of earth or uncut stone.
story:
Israel arrived at Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt (19:1). God offered them a covenant, promising that if they obeyed his voice they would be his treasured possession, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (19:5-6); the people agreed, consecrated themselves for three days, and on the third day the LORD descended on the mountain in fire, smoke, and thunder (19:16-19). Chapter 20 is what he says. These are the only words in the book that God speaks directly to the whole people. Everything else in the law comes through Moses, at the people's own request (verse 19), and Deuteronomy stresses that God spoke these words “to your whole assembly” and “added nothing more” (Deuteronomy 5:22).

The commandments open the long section of law that continues in the Book of the Covenant (20:22-23:33), which is read to the people and sealed in blood in the covenant ceremony of chapter 24. God later writes the words on two stone tablets (24:12; 31:18). Moses shatters them when Israel worships the golden calf (chapter 32), breaking the first two commandments within weeks, and receives new ones (chapter 34). Deuteronomy 5 repeats the commandments to the next generation on the edge of the land. From here on they are the heart of Israel's covenant, the words kept inside the ark itself (25:16; 1 Kings 8:9).
historical:
Law collections were known in the ancient Near East long before Israel. The laws of Ur-Nammu from Sumer (around 2100 BC), of Lipit-Ishtar of Isin (around 1930 BC), of the city of Eshnunna, and the Code of Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC) are the best known, and the laws of Exodus 21-23 share many of their concerns. The Ten Commandments are different in kind. Most ancient law is case law (if someone does this, then that follows), while the commandments are unconditional statements with no penalties attached, addressed to each Israelite as ‘you’. Albrecht Alt (Die Ursprünge des israelitischen Rechts, 1934) called this form apodictic law, contrasted it with casuistic or case law, and argued that it was distinctive of Israel; similar unconditional commands have since been identified in treaties and other texts, but no other ancient collection opens with a god's claim to exclusive worship.

In 1954 George Mendenhall (Covenant Forms in Israelite Tradition, Biblical Archaeologist 17) compared the Sinai covenant with Hittite treaties of the late second millennium BC, in which a great king names himself, recounts his past kindness to a subject people, lays down obligations, and provides for depositing the text and reading it publicly, with witnesses, blessings, and curses. Verse 2 fits the first two elements closely: a name, a history of rescue, then the demands, and the tablets placed in the ark answer to the deposited treaty text. Others, notably for Deuteronomy, have compared the covenant with Assyrian treaties of the seventh century BC such as the succession treaty of Esarhaddon (672 BC). The comparison does not settle the date, but it shows that the commandments are the terms of a relationship with a king who has already acted.

Archaeology shows how hard the first two commandments were to keep. Small clay figurines, especially the pillar figurines of a female figure common in Judahite houses of the eighth and seventh centuries BC, are found in large numbers. At Kuntillet Ajrud, a way station in the northern Sinai dated around 800 BC, inscriptions on storage jars invoke blessing by ‘Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah’ and ‘Yahweh of Teman and his Asherah’, which scholars read either as a goddess paired with Israel's God or as a cult object; either way they show the kind of worship the prophets condemned. The altar laws of verses 24-26 also have an archaeological echo: the Iron Age sanctuary excavated by Yohanan Aharoni at Arad in the Negev had an altar built of earth and unhewn stones.

The text of the commandments is attested early. The Nash Papyrus, a Hebrew sheet acquired in Egypt by W. L. Nash and published by Stanley Cook in 1903, now dated to the second or first century BC, contains the Decalogue in a form that blends Exodus and Deuteronomy, followed by the Shema. The Qumran scroll 4QDeutn (first century BC) gives the Sabbath command of Deuteronomy with the creation reason of Exodus 20:11 added, and several phylacteries found at Qumran contain the commandments. The Mishnah records that the priests in the temple recited the Ten Commandments daily with the Shema (m. Tamid 5:1).
cultural:
Several commandments cut against what was normal in Israel's world. Every neighboring people made images of its gods, and an image was not a mere picture. In Mesopotamia a ritual of ‘washing the mouth’ (mīs pî) was performed to bring a god's presence into a new statue, which was then clothed, fed, and carried in procession. Forbidding images meant that Israel's God could not be located, handled, or managed. Deuteronomy draws the reason from Sinai itself: “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12).

The command about taking the LORD's name in vain concerns more than careless speech. Names were invoked in oaths, curses, blessings, and magic, and the Hebrew speaks of lifting up the name ‘for emptiness’ (lashshav): using God's name to back a false oath, to curse, or to bend him to one's will. Israel's courts relied on oaths (22:10-11), so perjury in God's name attacked both God's honor and the justice of the community.

The Sabbath had no real parallel. Babylonian texts call the fifteenth day of the month, the full moon, shapattu, and some calendars treated the seventh, fourteenth, nineteenth, twenty-first, and twenty-eighth days as unlucky for certain activities, but a weekly day of rest extended to slaves, livestock, and resident foreigners appears in Israel alone. In a world where most people worked without pause, a law giving slaves a day off by divine command was startling, and the list in verse 10 is longer than for any other commandment because the Sabbath was most likely to be denied to those under someone else's authority.

The honor due to parents meant, for adults, provision and respect in old age, not only obedience in childhood, which is how Jesus applies it in Mark 7:9-13. Adultery in biblical law meant sexual relations with a woman married or betrothed to another man (Leviticus 20:10). The command against stealing has no object in Hebrew; the Talmud (Sanhedrin 86a) and Rashi read it as kidnapping, the theft of a person punished by death in 21:16, and Albrecht Alt argued the same in a well-known essay on the command, while most interpreters take it in its plain breadth. False witness belonged to the town gate, where cases were heard; the Code of Hammurabi opens with penalties for false accusation, and Israel's law gave the false witness the penalty he intended for his neighbor (Deuteronomy 19:16-19). The last commandment reaches past acts to desire, which no human court can enforce.

The altar laws of verses 24-26 reflect a plain worship. An altar of earth or of uncut stones (compare Joshua 8:31, “an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used”) kept human craft from the place of sacrifice, and the ban on steps protected the priest's modesty in the long robes of the day, a concern the priestly law later met with linen undergarments (28:42-43). The Mishnah says the stones of the Second Temple altar were never touched by iron, because iron shortens life and the altar lengthens it, and that the priests went up by a ramp (m. Middot 3:3-4).
literary:
The Bible never numbers these commands; it calls them ‘the ten words’ (aseret haddevarim, 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4), from which the Greek name Decalogue comes, and traditions divide them differently. Jewish tradition counts verse 2 as the first word and joins other gods and images (verses 3-6) as the second. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine (Questions on the Heptateuch 2.71), join other gods and images as the first commandment and divide coveting into two. Orthodox and Reformed Christians, following the older division found in Philo and Josephus (Antiquities 3.91-92) and in Origen, count other gods and images separately. The words are the same in every tradition; only the count differs. The traditions also divide the two tables differently: Philo put five commands on each, Augustine three and seven, Calvin four and six.

The commands fall into two groups, toward God and toward neighbor. The first group carries reasons and motives (verses 5-6, 7, 11, and the promise of verse 12), while most of the second are bare prohibitions, three of them only two words long in Hebrew (lo tirtsach, lo tin'af, lo tignov). The form lo with the imperfect is the Hebrew form of a permanent prohibition, ‘you shall never’, rather than a command for one occasion. The singular ‘you’ addresses the whole people as one and each Israelite personally.

Deuteronomy 5 gives a second version with differences a careful reader will notice: ‘remember’ the Sabbath becomes ‘observe’ it; the reason for the Sabbath is creation here (verse 11) and the exodus there (Deuteronomy 5:15); Deuteronomy puts the neighbor's wife before his house in the last command, gives her a separate verb, and adds his field; and it speaks of ‘empty’ rather than ‘false’ witness. The rabbis held that ‘remember’ and ‘observe’ were spoken in a single utterance (b. Shevuot 20b). Source critics take the differences as evidence of two traditions, with Exodus 20:11 reflecting the creation account of Genesis 1:1-2:3; others read Deuteronomy as Moses' later preaching of the same law.

The narrative frame matters. Verse 18 steps back to describe the people's experience of the voice they have just heard, and verse 19 records their request for a mediator, which Deuteronomy 18:15-18 remembers as the origin of the prophetic office. Then the Book of the Covenant opens, like the Decalogue itself, with God, idols, and the altar (verses 22-26), so that the whole body of law begins where the ten words began: with exclusive worship of the God who spoke.

outline.t: The LORD who brought Israel out of slavery
No other gods and no idols
Parents, life, marriage, property, truth, and desire
The people's fear and Moses the mediator
First laws of worship: no idols and a simple altar

doctrines.note: The commandments come after the rescue, and verse 2 grounds them in it. They describe the life of a people who belong to the God who freed them, guarding his honor and the neighbor's life, marriage, property, and name. The law is a gift given to the redeemed, not a ladder climbed to earn redemption, and the last command, aimed at desire, shows that it reaches the heart.

The first two commands forbid worshiping any other god and making any image to worship. The first guards God's uniqueness; the second keeps him from being shrunk to something people can make and manage. The reason is God's jealousy, the exclusive claim of a covenant partner (verse 5). Verse 23 repeats the warning at once, and chapter 32 shows how quickly it is broken.

The fourth command asks Israel to remember the seventh day and keep it holy, grounding it in God's own rest after creation (verse 11). The rest extends to children, slaves, animals, and resident foreigners (verse 10), so the Sabbath is both worship and protection for the weak. Christians differ over how the command applies after Christ, whether on the seventh day, on the Lord's Day as a Christian Sabbath, or as fulfilled in the rest Christ gives.

God names himself by his personal name, YHWH, revealed at the bush (3:14-15), and by an event: the one who brought Israel out of Egypt (verse 2). The third command protects that name from empty and false use, because the name stands for God himself as he has made himself known.

Moses tells the terrified people, “Do not be afraid”, and in the same breath says God has come “so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning” (verse 20). Scripture distinguishes the panic that drives people away from God from the reverent fear that keeps them near and obedient.

words.note: Davar, word, thing, matter, one of the most common nouns in the Old Testament (over 1,400 occurrences). Verse 1 introduces the commandments as haddevarim, ‘the words’, and the Bible's own name for them is ‘the ten words’ (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4), not ‘ten commandments’, though English versions often translate it so. The name stresses that they are speech from God addressed to a people, with verse 2 as the first ‘word’ in Jewish counting even though it commands nothing.

Qanna, jealous, used only six times in the Bible and always of God (20:5; 34:14 twice; Deuteronomy 4:24; 5:9; 6:15). It describes the passion of one who will not share what rightly belongs to him, the zeal of a husband for his marriage rather than petty envy. The prophets develop the image of Israel's idolatry as adultery (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3), and Exodus 34:14 goes further: “the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.”

Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, about 250 occurrences: loyalty that goes beyond what is owed. The Hebrew of verse 6 says la'alafim, ‘to thousands’, which the BSB and many versions take as ‘a thousand generations’ on the model of Deuteronomy 7:9. Either way the imbalance is deliberate: judgment reaches three or four generations of those who hate God; chesed reaches thousands of those who love him. Exodus 34:6-7 repeats the pair in God's own proclamation of his name.

Shav, emptiness, vanity, falsehood, about 53 occurrences. In verse 7, lashshav means ‘for emptiness’: using God's name for what is worthless or false. The same word describes the swearer of Psalm 24:4 who lifts up his soul to falsehood, which supports reading the command chiefly as a ban on false oaths, and Deuteronomy 5:20 uses it for ‘empty’ witness where Exodus 20:16 has sheqer, ‘false’.

Zakhar, to remember, about 230 occurrences. The fourth command opens with zakhor, an infinitive absolute used as a command (verse 8). In the Bible remembering is active: God ‘remembered’ his covenant and acted to save (2:24), and Israel remembers the Sabbath by keeping it holy. Deuteronomy 5:12 has shamor, ‘keep’ or ‘observe’, in the same place, and the Sabbath hymn Lekha Dodi opens with the rabbinic idea that both words were spoken at once.

Kaved, to be heavy, and in the Piel, as in kabbed (verse 12), ‘to give weight to, honor’. The verb occurs about 115 times, and the same root gives kavod, ‘glory’, the word for the glory of the LORD that settled on Sinai (24:16). Honoring parents is thus an act of the same kind, on a human scale, as glorifying God, and Paul notes that it is “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2).

Ratsach, to kill a person, about 47 occurrences. In the Old Testament it is used only of killing human beings, never of animals and never of killing in battle. It covers deliberate murder (1 Kings 21:19) and accidental manslaughter in the laws on cities of refuge (Numbers 35:11), and even the avenger who lawfully kills the manslayer (Numbers 35:27), so the verb names the act while the context supplies its moral quality. Most modern versions render the command ‘You shall not murder’, the King James Version ‘kill’.

Chamad, to desire, take pleasure in, covet, about 21 occurrences. It can describe desire alone, but several passages join it closely to taking: Achan ‘coveted and took’ (Joshua 7:21), and Micah condemns those who covet fields and seize them (Micah 2:2). Deuteronomy 5:21 pairs it with titavveh, ‘crave’. Paul quotes the command in the Greek form ouk epithymēseis as the one that exposed his own sin: “I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, ‘Do not covet’” (Romans 7:7).

christ:
Jesus did not set these commands aside. “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them,” he said of the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 5:17), and in the Sermon on the Mount he presses the commandments to the heart, treating contempt as a breach of the command against murder and lust as a breach of the command against adultery (Matthew 5:21-30), which is where the tenth commandment was already pointing. When a rich man asked what he must do to enter life, Jesus listed the commands of the second table (Matthew 19:17-19). Asked for the greatest commandment, he answered with love for God with all one's heart, soul, and mind, and love for one's neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37-40), the two tables of this chapter drawn from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. Paul says the commandments are summed up in “Love your neighbor as yourself” and that “love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:9-10); James argues from their unity that breaking one is breaking the law (James 2:10-11); and Ephesians 6:2-3 applies the fifth commandment to Christian households.

The New Testament also presents Christ as the answer to what Sinai could not do. Jeremiah had promised a new covenant in which God would put his law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and Paul calls the church a letter written “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). The people's plea for someone to stand between them and God's voice (verse 19) is remembered in Deuteronomy 18:15-18 as the origin of the promise of a prophet like Moses, which Peter applies to Jesus (Acts 3:22), and the New Testament names “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Hebrews contrasts the terror of Sinai with the approach believers now have to Mount Zion and “to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:18-24).

Two commandments take a particular shape in the light of Christ. The command against images (verse 4) forbids Israel to make a likeness of God, and the New Testament says that God has given his own image: the Son “is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). The Sabbath command is interpreted by Jesus as a gift, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath”, and he claims to be “Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27-28); Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9-10). Christians differ over what these mean for images in worship and for the weekly day (see the interpretation and the second hard question), but they agree that the commandments are now read through the one who fulfilled them.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition gave the ten words a special place and then guarded against overvaluing them. Philo of Alexandria's treatise On the Decalogue (early first century AD) arranged them in two tables of five and treated them as headings under which all the particular laws of the Torah could be gathered. The priests recited them daily in the temple (m. Tamid 5:1), but the Talmud reports that the recitation was dropped outside the temple because of the claims of the minim, sectarians who said that only the ten had been given at Sinai (b. Berakhot 12a). The Mekhilta (Bachodesh 5) explains why the commandments begin with ‘I am the LORD your God’ through a parable: a king who enters a province first builds its wall, brings in water, and fights its battles, and only then asks the people to accept his rule. The Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a) teaches that of the 613 commandments Israel heard the first two from God's own mouth. Maimonides, in a responsum, opposed standing for the reading of the Decalogue lest people think one part of the Torah more important than another, yet most congregations still stand when it is read in Parashat Yitro (Exodus 18:1-20:23) and on the first day of Shavuot, the feast that remembers Sinai.

Christian teachers treated the Decalogue as the church's moral catechism. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.15-16) held that its precepts are natural law, implanted in humanity from the beginning and extended rather than abolished by Christ; Augustine fixed the Western numbering; Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 100) argued that all the moral precepts of the old law are reducible to the Decalogue and belong to natural law. The Reformers made it one of the three pillars of instruction with the Creed and the Lord's Prayer: Luther's Small and Large Catechisms (1529), Calvin's Institutes (2.8), which called the guidance of believers the law's ‘third and principal use’ (2.7.12), the Heidelberg Catechism (1563, questions 92-115), which places the commandments under gratitude, and the Westminster Larger Catechism (questions 91-152). The Book of Common Prayer of 1552 had the priest read the commandments at Holy Communion, the people answering each one with a prayer for mercy and for hearts inclined to keep God's law. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) structures its moral teaching on the ten commandments. The command against images divided the church: the Second Council of Nicaea (787) approved the veneration of icons on the ground of the incarnation, while the Reformed churches (Heidelberg Catechism 96-98) rejected images in worship.

Modern scholarship has studied the form (Alt, 1934), the treaty background (Mendenhall, 1954), and the relation of the two versions, and has debated whether the ten are early or a late summary of Israel's law. In art and public life the chapter has had a long afterlife. Lucas Cranach and his workshop painted a Ten Commandments panel for the Wittenberg town council in 1516, Rembrandt painted Moses holding the tablets (1659), Cecil B. DeMille made the film The Ten Commandments (1956), and Krzysztof Kieślowski's ten films of Dekalog (1988) set each commandment in a Warsaw housing block. In the United States the posting of the commandments has repeatedly reached the Supreme Court, from Stone v. Graham (1980), which struck down a Kentucky classroom law, to Van Orden v. Perry and McCreary County v. ACLU (both 2005), decided on the same day with opposite results.
text:
Verse numbering differs between English Bibles and many Hebrew editions. The Masoretic Text carries two systems of accents in the Decalogue, one dividing it into verses of normal length and the other treating each commandment as a unit. In the numbering followed by some Hebrew editions and Jewish translations, including the JPS Tanakh (1985), the four short prohibitions of English verses 13-16 form a single verse 13, the command against coveting is verse 14, and the chapter ends at verse 23, so English 20:18-26 correspond to Hebrew 20:15-23. The words are the same.

The ancient witnesses show some real differences. The order of the commands against murder, adultery, and stealing varies: the Nash Papyrus, some Septuagint manuscripts including Codex Vaticanus, and Philo put adultery before murder, and so do Jesus in Luke 18:20, Paul in Romans 13:9, and James 2:11. The Septuagint of Exodus follows Deuteronomy in naming the neighbor's wife before his house in the last command. The Samaritan Pentateuch adds after verse 17 a command to build an altar on Mount Gerizim, drawing on Deuteronomy 27, and in verse 24 reads ‘where I have caused My name to be remembered’, a past form suited to its claim for Gerizim, where the Masoretic Text has an open future. Translation differences are also visible: ‘You shall not kill’ (KJV) and ‘You shall not murder’ (most modern versions) in verse 13; ‘to thousands’ (KJV) and ‘to a thousand generations’ (BSB, ESV) in verse 6; ‘graven image’ (KJV) and ‘idol’ or ‘carved image’ in verse 4; and in verse 5 ‘visiting’ (KJV, BSB) or ‘punishing’ (NIV) the iniquity of the fathers.

teach.big: The God who rescued Israel from slavery calls his freed people to exclusive loyalty to him and to a life that protects the neighbor, and he provides a mediator because sinful people cannot bear his voice alone.

outline.t: Grace comes before command: God names himself and what he has done before he says a word about what Israel must do.
The first loyalty is exclusive: no rival gods, and no image that shrinks God to something we can make, manage, or carry.
God's name is not a tool: invoking him to back a lie, a curse, or our own agenda treats him as empty.
Rest is holy time and a gift that reaches the weakest: the Sabbath patterns human life on God's work and protects those under authority.
Love for the neighbor guards his parents, life, marriage, freedom and goods, reputation, and even what we allow ourselves to want.
Fear that drives people away is answered by a mediator and turned into reverent fear that keeps them from sin.
Worship is shaped by how God has revealed himself, by voice and not by form, and he promises to come and bless where he makes his name known.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misreading turns the commandments into a ladder to God, as if keeping them were the way to earn his favor. Verse 2 puts rescue first; the commandments are the shape of life for a people already freed. The opposite error treats them as obsolete for Christians because of grace, although Jesus and the apostles repeat and deepen them. A third error reduces them to outward rules that a respectable person can easily keep. Jesus' reading in Matthew 5 and the tenth commandment itself show that they reach the heart.

Teachers should also be careful with particular commands. The command against taking the LORD's name in vain is often reduced to a ban on swearing; its core is using God's name to back falsehood or manipulation, which religious people are especially prone to. The fifth command is sometimes used to demand that adult children submit to abusive parents; it calls for honor and care, not for tolerating abuse. The sixth is sometimes cited on its own to settle debates about war, capital punishment, or self-defense, where Christians hold different positions and the verb's usage does not decide the matter. Finally, a public display of the commandments is not the same as keeping them, and preaching that treats them chiefly as a cultural symbol misses the relationship they describe.
teach.pastoral: The commandments will press on people carrying guilt: those who have committed adultery, stolen, lied in ways that damaged others, or ended a life. Teach them with verse 2 in view, as the words of a God who rescues, and let the mediator of verses 19-21 point to the forgiveness the gospel offers, so that conviction does not become despair. Scrupulous people may hear the tenth command as proof that every passing desire condemns them; it is right to say that the command aims at settled craving that plans to take, not at every temptation that crosses the mind. The fifth command needs special care in any room that includes people who were abused or neglected by their parents. Honor can mean truthfulness, boundaries, and care from a safe distance, and it never requires returning to harm. The seventh command will touch the divorced and the betrayed; teach it without shaming those who were sinned against.

hard.q: Is a jealous God who visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children worthy of worship?
hard.a:
The objection has an ancient and a modern form. Marcion in the second century contrasted the jealous, punishing God of the law with the God of love revealed in Jesus, and Richard Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006) opened a chapter by calling the Old Testament God jealous and proud of it, among many harsher charges. The moral problem is sharpened by the Bible itself. Verse 5 says God visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generations, yet Deuteronomy 24:16 says “each is to die for his own sin”, and Ezekiel forbids the proverb about sour grapes and declares, “The soul who sins is the one who will die” (Ezekiel 18:2-3, 20).

Jewish interpreters addressed the tension early. Targum Onqelos translates verse 5 as applying to the children who continue to sin after their fathers, and the Talmud (Berakhot 7a) reconciles Exodus and Deuteronomy the same way: the punishment falls on children who take hold of their fathers' deeds as their own. The verse's own qualifier supports this, since it speaks of “those who hate Me”. Others note that three or four generations was the span of a household living together in the ancient world, so the verse describes how one generation's idolatry damages everyone under its roof, a pattern visible in families still, and that Ezekiel was answering exiles who used the principle to blame their ancestors instead of repenting.

On jealousy, many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, point out that the word describes a husband's rightful passion for his marriage, not insecurity or spite (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3), and that indifference to a beloved's unfaithfulness would be a lesser love, not a greater one. The verse is also lopsided by design: judgment reaches a few generations of those who hate God, and loving devotion reaches thousands of those who love him, a proportion Exodus 34:6-7 repeats in God's own proclamation of his name. Readers who reject the God of the Bible will not be persuaded by these answers, and a reader should know that the dispute turns on whether exclusive claims can be loving. The church confesses that the jealous God of Sinai is the same God who is love (1 John 4:8), and that in Christ his jealousy for his people takes the form of self-giving.

hard.q: Are Christians bound by the Ten Commandments, and especially by the Sabbath?
hard.a:
The sharpest objection comes from the text and from Jewish readers. The commandments are addressed to the people God brought out of Egypt (verse 2), as part of a covenant with Israel, and they include the seventh-day Sabbath, which most Christians do not keep. The Talmud's worry about sectarians who claimed that only the ten were binding (b. Berakhot 12a) and Maimonides' refusal to single them out both reflect a Jewish conviction that the Decalogue cannot be lifted out of the whole Torah. On this view Christians who claim the ten while dropping the Sabbath and the rest of the law are being selective. Christians themselves disagree, and the main positions deserve to be stated as their holders would.

Seventh-day Christians, among them Seventh Day Baptists and Seventh-day Adventists, hold that all ten remain binding in their original form, including rest on the seventh day, since Jesus kept the Sabbath and the command is grounded in creation (verse 11), before Israel existed. The Reformed and Puritan tradition, expressed in the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21), holds that the Decalogue is the permanent moral law and that the Sabbath principle continues, transferred by Christ's resurrection to the first day of the week as the Christian Sabbath or Lord's Day. Catholic, Lutheran, and many other Christians hold that the moral substance of the commandments is permanent and is natural law (Irenaeus; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 100), while the specific seventh-day rest was a ceremonial sign fulfilled in Christ; Luther's Large Catechism reads the third commandment chiefly as a call to hear God's word, and the church keeps Sunday as the day of resurrection. A fourth view, found in some dispensational and New Covenant theologians, holds that the Mosaic covenant as a whole has ended in Christ, that believers are under the law of Christ, and that nine of the ten are restated in the New Testament while the Sabbath is not, pointing to Colossians 2:16-17 and Romans 14:5.

All these positions agree that Jesus affirmed the commandments' moral demands and deepened them, and that salvation is not earned by keeping them. They differ over how the covenant with Israel relates to the church, a second-order question on which faithful Christians have disagreed since the early centuries. Many Jewish readers, for their part, see in the Christian debate a confirmation that the commandments belong first to Israel, and Christians who teach them honor the text by remembering that they were first spoken to a people brought out of Egypt.

observe: What does God say about himself in verse 2 before he gives any command?
Which commandments include a reason or a promise, and what are those reasons?
How do the people respond to the thunder and the voice in verses 18-21, and what does Moses tell them?
interpret: Why do you think the commandments begin with God's act of rescue rather than with a demand? How does that change the meaning of obedience?
Why would God forbid images of himself when every neighboring people had them? What does an image do to the way people think about God?
Moses says both ‘Do not be afraid’ and that God has come ‘so that the fear of Him may be before you’ (verse 20). What two kinds of fear is he distinguishing?
apply: The tenth commandment reaches past actions to desire. Which of the other commandments do you think is usually broken first in the heart, and where do you see that in your own life?
The Sabbath gave rest even to slaves, animals, and foreigners. What would it look like for your rest to protect the rest of other people?
Where are you tempted to use God's name, or the language of faith, to back your own agenda?
